title: Yet they mean practical intellect: assent moves the will by effects
source_text: IV. Verum hic per intellectum, non mentem theoreticam sed practicam intelligunt: quandoquidem fidei proprium actum esse docent, non assensum quemvis, sed assensum practicum, qui voluntatem movet atque afficit. Ac proinde quamvis existiment fidem subjective esse in solo intellectu, illam tamen volunt esse in voluntate effective, id est, per suos effectus. Nempe, quia licet proprius ejus actus in mente recipiatur, multos tamen illa motus & operationes in voluntate excitat, quae necessario illam comitantur, & sine quibus vera & salvifica fides nec esse, nec dici meretur.
pass_a_gloss: But here by intellect they understand not the theoretical but the practical mind: since they teach that the proper act of faith is not any assent whatever, but practical assent, which moves and affects the will. And therefore although they judge faith to be subjectively in the intellect alone, they nevertheless want it to be in the will effectively, that is, by its effects. Namely, because although its proper act is received in the mind, it nevertheless excites many motions and operations in the will which necessarily accompany it, and without which true and saving faith neither is nor deserves to be called such.
pass_b_english: Intellect here = practical mind: faith's proper act is practical assent that moves the will.
Subjectively in intellect alone, yet effectively in the will by inseparable effects.
